domain: International Political Economy / Monetary History / International Law
topic_summary: Analysis of the Bretton Woods Agreement's dollar-gold convertibility framework as a contested kernel. Two primary readings emerge: strict convertibility (binding obligation constraining U.S. monetary expansion, benefiting creditor nations) versus policy-flexible interpretation (prioritizing domestic stability, enabling suspension as in 1971, shifting burdens to dollar holders). The analytical question centers on whether these represent genuinely different constraint structures or merely different policy preferences within a single constraint.

key_entities: United States (hegemon, reserve currency issuer, debtor by 1960s)
Bretton Woods Agreement 1944 (founding treaty establishing dollar-gold convertibility at $35/oz)
Creditor Nations (France, Germany, others demanding gold conversion)
International Monetary Fund (institutional arbiter, enforcement mechanism)
Gold Standard (pre-existing commitment system, template for Bretton Woods)
key_tensions: U.S. domestic monetary autonomy vs international convertibility obligation
Creditor nations' legal claims vs U.S. strategic interests (Cold War financing, Great Society programs)
key_mechanisms: Article IV convertibility obligation (treaty mechanism linking dollar to gold)
Gold window (operational mechanism: foreign central banks exchange dollars for gold at Fed)
Nixon Shock August 1971 (unilateral suspension, treaty breach vs force majeure)
key_absences: Enforcement mechanism for convertibility breach — IMF lacked credible sanction power against hegemon
Adjustment mechanism for structural U.S. deficits — Triffin dilemma not addressed in treaty design

axiom_contradictions.basis: Strict convertibility axiom holds treaty obligation as supreme constraint on monetary sovereignty; policy-flexible axiom holds domestic stability as trump card against external commitments. No coherent framework simultaneously treats both as foundational—accepting one as true requires rejecting the other's priority claim.

Triffin axiom holds the system was structurally impossible from inception (contradiction between liquidity provision and convertibility maintenance); strict convertibility axiom holds the treaty obligation was coherent and enforceable. A framework holding Triffin's structural impossibility cannot simultaneously hold that strict enforcement was feasible.

omegas.description: Do strict_convertibility and policy_flexible readings collapse into one constraint (treaty obligation) with two observer positions (creditor vs debtor)? Independence test: they emit different epsilon bins and victim sets, but share the treaty text as observable. Bounded as genuine kernel per §1.3-K, but collapse risk noted.

Is Triffin dilemma a true Mountain (mathematical constraint on any reserve currency system) or a Rope (coordination failure solvable via SDR-like mechanisms)? Classification affects whether it constrains future digital currency regimes.

Extraction cataloged enforcement mechanism absence (§1.1). Does this absence convert strict_convertibility_reading from Rope to Scaffold (unenforceable norm)? If so, the kernel contest may be asymmetric: one reading enforceable (policy_flexible via unilateral action), one not.
